title: Regular Expressions (regexp)
summary: The **regexp** package matches text against patterns using Google's **RE2** engine — which guarantees linear-time matching but drops backreferences and lookarounds. You **compile once** (usually `regexp.MustCompile` at package scope) and reuse the `*regexp.Regexp` for `MatchString`, `FindStringSubmatch`, `ReplaceAllString`, and more.

subtopics.title: Compile once, reuse
subtopics.explanation: Compiling a pattern is expensive, so build the Regexp once — typically a package-level variable with regexp.MustCompile — and reuse it. MustCompile panics on an invalid pattern (fine for constant patterns known at build time); regexp.Compile returns an error for patterns built at runtime.

subtopics.title: Matching and finding
subtopics.explanation: MatchString reports whether the pattern occurs. FindString returns the leftmost match (empty string if none). FindAllString returns every non-overlapping match; the second argument caps how many (-1 for all). For a plain substring, strings.Contains is faster than a regexp.

subtopics.title: Capture groups
subtopics.explanation: Parentheses create capture groups. FindStringSubmatch returns a slice whose element 0 is the whole match and 1..n are the groups. A nil result means no match, so guard for it before indexing.

subtopics.title: Named groups
subtopics.explanation: Name a group with (?P<name>...) and pair FindStringSubmatch with SubexpNames to look groups up by name instead of position — clearer and resilient to reordering.

subtopics.title: Replacing text
subtopics.explanation: ReplaceAllString swaps every match. In the replacement, $1 (or ${name}) inserts a captured group; use $$ for a literal dollar sign. ReplaceAllStringFunc lets you compute each replacement in Go code.

foundations.overview: regexp compiles a pattern into a reusable Regexp value and offers a family of methods that either test (MatchString), extract (FindString, FindStringSubmatch, FindAllString), or rewrite (ReplaceAllString) text. Patterns use RE2 syntax, which trades away backreferences and lookaround in exchange for a guarantee of linear-time matching — no catastrophic backtracking. The core discipline is: compile once, reuse the value, and guard submatch results for nil.
foundations.formalDefinition: regexp implements regular-expression search using the RE2 engine, matching the syntax accepted by egrep/PCRE minus features that would break the linear-time guarantee (backreferences, lookahead/lookbehind). A compiled pattern is a *regexp.Regexp, safe for concurrent use by multiple goroutines.
foundations.whyItMatters: Validation, log parsing, tokenizing, and search-and-replace are everyday tasks. Knowing RE2's guarantees (and limits), compiling once, and reading submatches correctly avoids both performance pitfalls and subtle extraction bugs.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a compiled Regexp as a prebuilt, reusable machine: building it costs work, so you build it once and feed many strings through it. Submatch results are positional — index 0 is 'the whole thing', and each opening parenthesis, left to right, is the next slot.
commonUseCases: Extracting fields from log lines with capture groups
Normalizing whitespace or redacting text with ReplaceAll

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go regexp supports backreferences like \1 and lookahead.
commonMisconceptions.reality: RE2 deliberately omits them to guarantee linear time. If you need them, restructure the problem or use a parser instead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should compile the pattern wherever you use it.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Compiling in a loop or per-request is wasteful; compile once into a package var (MustCompile) and reuse it — it's goroutine-safe.

commonMisconceptions.myth: FindStringSubmatch always returns a non-empty slice.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It returns nil when there's no match; indexing m[1] then panics. Check m != nil first.

visualExplorer.title: How FindStringSubmatch fills the result slice
visualExplorer.caption: Element 0 is the full match; each capture group, left to right, is the next element.

steps.name: Scan for the leftmost match
steps.detail: The engine finds '2024-03' — the leftmost substring the whole pattern matches.

steps.name: No match → nil
steps.detail: On a string with no match, the result is nil, not an empty-but-usable slice — so guard before indexing.

interactiveExamples.title: Find all vs find first
interactiveExamples.explanation: FindString returns only the leftmost match; FindAllString(-1) returns every non-overlapping match as a slice.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: pull the year out of a date
interactiveExamples.explanation: Add a capture group around the 4-digit year, then read it from FindStringSubmatch. Remember index 0 is the whole match.

checkpoints.explanation: \d+ matches maximal runs of digits, so the three runs are "1", "22", "333"; FindAllString(-1) returns them all as a []string, which prints as [1 22 333].

checkpoints.prompt: Where should a constant pattern be compiled in a web service?
options: Inside the request handler, each request
Once in a package-level var via regexp.MustCompile
Inside a for loop over inputs
It doesn't matter, compiling is free
checkpoints.explanation: Compiling is relatively expensive and the result is goroutine-safe, so compile once at package scope with MustCompile and reuse it across all requests rather than recompiling per call.

checkpoints.prompt: This panics on some inputs. Why?
options: When input has no match, FindStringSubmatch returns nil and m[1] panics with index out of range
You must call MatchString first always
checkpoints.explanation: On a non-matching input the result is nil; indexing m[1] then panics. Guard with `if m != nil {` (or `len(m) > 1`) before reading a group.

checkpoints.prompt: Collapse any run of whitespace into a single space.
checkpoints.explanation: ReplaceAllString(src, repl) replaces every match of \s+ with a single space, producing "a b c". FindString/MatchString don't rewrite; Split would return the pieces, not a joined string.

codeLab.title: Extract all integers from text
codeLab.instructions: Implement `ExtractInts(s string) []int` that returns every integer in s, in order, including negative numbers (e.g. "a-5 b12" -> [-5, 12]). Use a compiled regexp and strconv.Atoi. Return an empty (non-nil) slice when there are none.
hints: The pattern -?\d+ captures an optional minus then one or more digits.
make([]int, 0, n) returns a non-nil empty slice so the 'no numbers' case matches []int{}.

debuggingLab.title: Log parser is far slower than expected
debuggingLab.symptom: A function that validates millions of lines spends most of its time inside regexp.Compile.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The pattern is a compile-time constant, but MustCompile runs on every call, rebuilding the same automaton millions of times. Compilation dominates the runtime even though matching itself is cheap.
commonMistakes: Compiling a constant pattern inside a hot function or loop.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Hoist the compiled pattern to a package-level variable so it's built once.

theory.question: What is the difference between regexp.Compile and regexp.MustCompile?
theory.directAnswer: Both build a *regexp.Regexp from a pattern. Compile returns (*Regexp, error) so you can handle an invalid pattern at runtime — use it when the pattern comes from user input or config. MustCompile returns just the *Regexp and panics if the pattern is invalid — use it for constant patterns known at build time, typically assigned to a package-level variable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two constructors for a compiled regular expression differing in error handling.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Constant patterns should fail fast and loudly at startup (MustCompile); dynamic patterns need graceful error handling (Compile).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: MustCompile calls Compile and panics on error; both produce a Regexp that is safe for concurrent use.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing correctly prevents either unhandled runtime panics (dynamic pattern with MustCompile) or noisy error plumbing for constants.
theory.realWorldExample: A package-level var email = regexp.MustCompile(...) for a fixed format; regexp.Compile(userFilter) when a user supplies a search pattern.

followUps.question: Is a compiled Regexp safe to share across goroutines?
followUps.answer: Yes — a *regexp.Regexp is immutable after compilation and safe for concurrent use, which is exactly why compiling once and sharing is the norm.

theory.question: Why doesn't Go's regexp support backreferences or lookahead?
theory.directAnswer: Go uses the RE2 engine, which guarantees matching in linear time relative to the input length. Backreferences and lookaround can't be supported without risking exponential (catastrophic) backtracking, so RE2 omits them by design. The payoff is predictable performance and no ReDoS vulnerability from a crafted input.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A deliberate feature trade-off in the RE2 engine Go's regexp is built on.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make regex matching safe and fast even on adversarial input, at the cost of a few advanced features.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: RE2 compiles to an automaton executed in O(n) time; features needing backtracking are excluded to preserve that bound.

theory.whyImportant: It affects both what patterns you can write and why Go regex is safe against ReDoS — a common security topic.
theory.realWorldExample: A public API accepting user regex filters is safe from ReDoS specifically because Go uses RE2.

followUps.question: What do you do when you truly need a backreference?
followUps.answer: Restructure the task (e.g., capture then compare in Go code), or use a dedicated parser; a general regex isn't the right tool there.

scenario.question: A teammate validates emails with a huge regex and reports occasional slowness and a few false rejections. How do you approach it in Go?
scenario.directAnswer: First, since Go uses RE2, the slowness isn't catastrophic backtracking — profile to confirm it's likely per-call compilation, and hoist the pattern to a package var. Second, for email specifically, a giant regex is the wrong tool: prefer net/mail.ParseAddress for correctness, or a deliberately simple pattern plus a confirmation step. Over-strict regexes reject valid addresses, so relax the pattern and verify deliverability out of band.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A validation-design and performance question around regex misuse.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Email grammar is more complex than a readable regex can capture, and recompilation is a common perf bug.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: net/mail parses per the RFC; compiling once removes the per-call cost; a confirmation email is the real correctness check.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows judgment about when NOT to use regex and how to reason about Go regex performance.
scenario.realWorldExample: Switching signup validation from a 200-char email regex to net/mail.ParseAddress plus a confirmation link cut false rejections to near zero.

followUps.question: How would you confirm compilation was the bottleneck?
followUps.answer: Benchmark the hot path with testing.B before and after hoisting the compile out, and check a pprof CPU profile for regexp.Compile.

systemDesign.question: Design a configurable log-redaction layer in Go that strips secrets (tokens, emails, card numbers) from log lines before they leave the process.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Load a set of named rules from config, each with a pattern and a replacement, and compile them once at startup with regexp.Compile (returning errors so a bad rule fails the boot, not a request). Represent the redactor as a slice of {name, *regexp.Regexp, replacement}. Expose Redact(line string) string that applies each rule's ReplaceAllString in order. Because Go uses RE2, user/config-supplied patterns can't cause ReDoS. Wrap the process logger so every line passes through Redact, and add golden tests per rule.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A pipeline of precompiled regex rules applied to every outgoing log line.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Leaking secrets to logs is a common, serious incident; centralizing redaction makes it consistent and auditable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Rules compile once at startup (Compile so a bad rule is caught early); Redact runs each ReplaceAllString; the logger middleware calls Redact before writing.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It combines compile-once discipline, RE2's safety with untrusted patterns, and clean layering — a realistic production concern.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A service redacts Authorization tokens and PANs from structured logs via a compiled rule set loaded from a redaction.yaml.

followUps.question: Why compile config patterns with Compile, not MustCompile?
followUps.answer: Config is runtime input; Compile lets a malformed rule fail startup with a clear error instead of panicking deep in request handling.

followUps.question: How do you keep redaction from wrecking log throughput?
followUps.answer: Compile once, keep the rule list short and anchored, and benchmark; for very hot paths, gate redaction to fields likely to contain secrets.

followUps.question: What's a correctness risk of regex redaction?
followUps.answer: Over-broad patterns can mangle legitimate text, and over-narrow ones miss secrets; golden tests and periodic review balance the two.

coding.question: Implement `func Slugify(title string) string` that lowercases the title, replaces every run of non-alphanumeric characters with a single hyphen, and trims leading/trailing hyphens (e.g. "  Hello, World!  " -> "hello-world").
coding.thoughtProcess: Lowercase first with strings.ToLower. Then use one compiled regexp [^a-z0-9]+ to collapse every run of non-alphanumeric characters into a single hyphen via ReplaceAllString. Finally strip any leading/trailing hyphens with strings.Trim. Compiling the pattern once at package scope keeps it efficient.
coding.lineByLine: strings.ToLower normalizes case so the class [a-z0-9] suffices. The compiled pattern [^a-z0-9]+ matches maximal runs of anything that isn't a lowercase letter or digit; ReplaceAllString turns each run into a single '-'. Leading/trailing separators (from spaces or punctuation at the ends) are removed with strings.Trim, yielding a clean slug like "hello-world".

followUps.question: Why lowercase before the regexp instead of using [^a-zA-Z0-9]+?
followUps.answer: Lowercasing first means the slug is already normalized and the class stays simple; it also handles mixed-case runs consistently.

followUps.question: How would you support Unicode letters (e.g. accented characters)?
followUps.answer: Use the Unicode class in the pattern (e.g. [^\p{L}\p{N}]+) and optionally transliterate accents first; RE2 supports \p{L}/\p{N}.

keyTakeaways: Compile once and reuse: put constant patterns in a package-level var via regexp.MustCompile (goroutine-safe); use regexp.Compile for runtime/user patterns so you can handle errors.
FindStringSubmatch returns [wholeMatch, group1, …] or nil on no match — always guard before indexing a group.
Go uses RE2: linear-time matching but no backreferences or lookaround, which also makes it safe from ReDoS on untrusted input.
ReplaceAllString rewrites every match and supports $1/${name} in the replacement; for plain substrings prefer strings.Contains/Replace over a regexp.
